subject: PSHE & RSE
source: National Curriculum / statutory RSHE guidance (Relationships Education, Health Education); PSHE Association programme of study themes; TGA RSHE Policy 2026-27 and TGA RECIPE Character Framework 2026-27 (Drive); Drive PSHE folder (PSHE Association KS3 'Healthy coping strategies' lesson) adapted for Y8.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Me, my family and my friends
lessons.title: The people who care for me
objectives: Name people who care for us
Say how families look after each other
Say thank you to the people who care for us

keywords.def: people who love and look after us
to look after someone and be kind
an adult you can ask for help
words we say to show we are grateful

starter: Bismillah. What is your name? Say it nicely.
Name one thing you like to do.

teach.heading: Our class rules
teach.note: Say bismillah. Keep it very short and calm. Do not ask children to share anything about home that they do not wish to share. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Pupils may ask anonymous questions via the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Families care for us
bullets: Families can be big or small
Grown-ups feed us and keep us safe
Allah tells us to be kind to our parents
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 17:23 says to be kind and good to parents. Families look different; accept all answers without comment.

teach.heading: Trusted grown-ups
bullets: Tell them if you feel worried
teach.note: Ask: who would you ask for help? Stress that we always tell a grown-up if we feel unsafe.

teach.heading: Saying thank you
bullets: Give it to someone who helps you
teach.note: Teach the phrase; explain it is a way of thanking someone. Plan a thank you card with colouring.

practice: Name one person who looks after you (just their role, for example Mummy).
What do we say when someone helps us?
independent: Draw a person who helps you and colour the picture.
exit: Draw and decorate a thank-you card for someone who cares for you.
Say thank you to someone at home.
homework: What can you say to thank someone?
lessons.send: Give your thank-you card to someone at home and say jazakAllahu khayran.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Me, my family and my friends
lessons.title: Being a good friend

keywords.def: someone who is kind to you and plays with you
to let someone else have a turn or a part
words we say when we hurt someone

starter: Bismillah. Who looks after you at home? (a grown-up's role only)
Show me a kind hand, not a hitting hand.

teach.heading: Kind friends
bullets: Help a friend who is sad
teach.note: Model saying 'As-salamu alaykum'. Praise any kind idea. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said that the best of you are those best in character (Sahih al-Bukhari).

teach.heading: Sharing and turns
teach.note: Role-play with puppets or toys. Ask: How does it feel to wait? How does it feel when someone shares?

teach.heading: Saying sorry
bullets: If we hurt someone, we say sorry
teach.note: Teach 'I am sorry. Are you okay?' Misconception: sorry means you are bad. Sorry shows kindness.

teach.heading: Friendship pictures
bullets: Say what kind words they say
teach.note: Use shapes or stick figures if children wish; do not draw faces if the family prefers. Colour with care.

practice: Say a kind sentence to a friend.
What do we do when we hurt someone?
independent: Role-play sharing a toy with a friend.
exit: Draw a kind friend and say how they were kind.
Tell a grown-up one way you can be kind tomorrow.
homework: Name one way to be a good friend.
What do we say when we hurt someone?
lessons.send: Do one kind thing for someone at home and tell the class next time.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: My feelings and staying safe
lessons.title: My feelings
objectives: Name feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared, calm
Say what helps when we feel upset

keywords.def: how you feel inside, like happy or sad
a strong, hot feeling when something is unfair
to take air in and let it out slowly

starter: Bismillah. Show me a happy face.
What do we say when we hurt someone?

teach.heading: Feelings are okay
bullets: All feelings are okay to have
teach.note: Show picture cards of feelings (faces are used here as emotion cards, symbols only). Ask which feelings children know.

teach.heading: What helps?
bullets: Ask for a hug or help
Tell a grown-up how you feel
teach.note: Model 'smell the flower, blow the candle'. Praise 'calm' attempts.

teach.heading: Dua and feeling calm
bullets: We can say 'Bismillah' before we start
We can say 'Alhamdulillah' when things are good
teach.note: Keep it simple. Avoid promising that feelings disappear; focus on coping.

teach.heading: Feelings in a bag
teach.note: Pupils draw circles with colours that match feelings (no faces needed).

practice: How do you feel today? Use a colour.
What do you do when you feel cross?
exit: Make a feelings chart with four colours and words.
Tell a grown-up one thing that helps you feel calm.
homework: What can you do when you feel upset?
lessons.send: Practise slow breaths with a family member before bedtime.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: My feelings and staying safe
lessons.title: Staying safe with screens
objectives: Say a grown-up must know when we use a screen
Know not to share names or pictures with strangers
Tell a grown-up if something worries us

keywords.def: a tablet, phone or computer you look at
to say something to a grown-up

starter: Bismillah. Name something you can watch on a screen.
Who can help if you feel worried?

teach.heading: Screens can be fun and safe
bullets: We learn and play on screens
A grown-up should be with us
We only use apps we are allowed
teach.note: Ask: what do you do on a screen? Keep a positive tone. Acknowledge the school live lesson is also a screen.

teach.heading: Staying safe
bullets: Never share your name or address
Never talk to people you do not know
teach.note: Role-play: a pop-up asks 'What is your name?'. Children say 'I will ask a grown-up'.

teach.heading: Worried? Tell a grown-up
bullets: Close the screen or turn it off
You will not be in trouble
teach.note: Stress they will not be in trouble. This is the key safety message. Offer a 'stop, tell' hand gesture.

practice: What do you do before using a tablet?
Who do you tell if something worries you?
independent: Act out what to do when a pop-up asks your name.
Draw a stop sign for 'tell a grown-up'.
exit: Draw a safe screen picture with a grown-up beside the child.
homework: What do you do if something worries you on a screen?
Do we share our name with strangers?
lessons.send: Tell a grown-up your three screen rules and ask them to help you remember.
